node.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
node.period_rationale: Allen (1971) opens the field inside “Reorientations, c. 1970–85”; the secularization debate (1985–96) runs through period_3. The Catholic Action revision (2002–05) is now a strand of quebec_historiography.
node.date_label: Allen, The Social Passion 1971 · Cook, The Regenerators 1985 · secularization debate: Gauvreau 1991, Marshall 1992 and 1993–94, Christie and Gauvreau 1996 · coverage through 2000; post-2000 extension partial

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. Earlier denominational and church histories are not counted; 1971 is the first selected work, 2017 the latest. Neither bounds the field.

node.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.
node.scope_note: A research field containing a debate. “Secularization thesis” is the name its critics gave to Cook’s and Marshall’s accounts (Laverdure’s 1998 review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept in 1993–94. Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in quebec_historiography, reached from here by the contribution edge crr_rel_04. Moral reform as regulation (Valverde) is placed in moral_regulation.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Allen, The Social Passion (1971); Cook, The Regenerators (1985); Van Die, An Evangelical Mind (1989); Westfall, Two Worlds (1989); Gauvreau, The Evangelical Century (1991); Marshall, Secularizing the Faith (1992) and “Canadian Historians, Secularization and the Problem of the Nineteenth Century” (1993–94); Christie and Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996); Marks, Revivals and Roller Rinks (1996); Semple, The Lord’s Dominion (1996); Hamelin and Gagnon, Histoire du catholicisme québécois: Le XXe siècle (1984); Perin, Rome in Canada (1990); McGowan, The Waning of the Green (1999); Ferretti (1999); Hubert (2000); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005; strand in quebec_historiography); Christie and Gauvreau, Christian Churches and Their Peoples (2010); Marks, Infidels and the Damn Churches (2017). Comparison: Brown, The Death of Christian Britain (2001).

representative_people.name: Richard Allen
representative_people.context: The Social Passion made the social gospel and its reform movements a central subject of Canadian religious and political history.

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Reads late Victorian social criticism through Darwinism, higher criticism, positivism and social Christianity as “the sacred becomes the secular”; with Marshall, named by Christie and Gauvreau’s reviewer as the strongest advocate of “the secularization thesis” they challenged. Primary placement in intellectual and cultural history.

representative_people.name: David B. Marshall
representative_people.context: Traces Protestant clergy’s crisis of belief, with the 1920s as “an era of drift”, in what he calls a “long-term incremental model”; in 1993–94 he defended the concept against Gauvreau: “Attempts to dismiss the concept of secularization are premature.” His critics call his and Cook’s position the secularization thesis.
representative_people.works: Secularizing the Faith (1992); “Canadian Historians, Secularization and the Problem of the Nineteenth Century” (1993–94)

representative_people.name: Michael Gauvreau
representative_people.context: Reassesses Cook’s account of the evangelical creed and argues with Christie that the Protestant churches gained influence before 1940. His Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005) is now treated in the Catholic Action strand of quebec_historiography, linked from here by crr_rel_04.
representative_people.works: The Evangelical Century (1991); A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), with Nancy Christie; The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005)

representative_people.name: Nancy Christie
representative_people.context: With Gauvreau, challenges the decline thesis and writes a social history of churches and their peoples; argues that religion helped build the liberal order.
representative_people.works: A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), with Michael Gauvreau; Households of Faith (2001), ed.; Christian Churches and Their Peoples (2010), with Michael Gauvreau

representative_people.name: William Westfall
representative_people.context: Protestant culture in nineteenth-century Ontario; title-level only here.

representative_people.name: Marguerite Van Die
representative_people.context: Writes on Nathanael Burwash and the Methodist tradition, on women and "separate spheres" in religious families, and later distinguishes political from social secularization in a liberal state.
representative_people.works: An Evangelical Mind (1989); “Revisiting ‘Separate Spheres’” in Households of Faith (2001); “Protestants, the Liberal State, and the Practice of Politics” (2014)

representative_people.name: Neil Semple
representative_people.context: A full history of Canadian Methodism arguing it became "the most Canadian of all the churches".

representative_people.name: Lynne Marks
representative_people.context: Moves the question to lived religion: class, gender and leisure in Ontario towns, and irreligion shaped by class and race in settler British Columbia.
representative_people.works: Revivals and Roller Rinks (1996); Infidels and the Damn Churches (2017)

representative_people.name: Jean Hamelin
representative_people.context: Coauthor of the twentieth-century volume of the standard history of Quebec Catholicism.
representative_people.works: Histoire du catholicisme québécois: Le XXe siècle (1984), with Nicole Gagnon

representative_people.name: Nicole Gagnon
representative_people.context: Coauthor with Jean Hamelin; metadata only.
representative_people.works: Histoire du catholicisme québécois: Le XXe siècle (1984)

representative_people.name: Roberto Perin
representative_people.context: The Vatican and Canadian affairs in the late Victorian age; title-level only.

representative_people.name: Mark G. McGowan
representative_people.context: Irish Catholics and identity in Toronto; title-level only.

representative_people.name: Lucia Ferretti
representative_people.context: A short francophone synthesis of the Catholic Church in Quebec; metadata only.
representative_people.works: Brève histoire de l’Église catholique au Québec (1999)

representative_people.name: Ollivier Hubert
representative_people.context: The Church's management of rites in Quebec; Christie names his work among studies of religion and the liberal order.
representative_people.works: Sur la terre comme au ciel (2000)

representative_people.name: Callum G. Brown
representative_people.context: British comparison: secularization as a sudden rupture of the 1960s rather than a long decline; heavily co-cited with A Full-Orbed Christianity in Canadian PhDs.

representative_people.name: Mariana Valverde
representative_people.context: Moral reform as central to race, class and gender in English Canada; the boundary with moral regulation, where she has her primary placement.
representative_people.works: The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991)

strands.title: The social gospel and reform
strands.focus: Protestant social Christianity as a reform movement between the 1880s and 1920s.
strands.works: Allen, The Social Passion (1971); Cook, The Regenerators (1985)

strands.title: Crisis of belief and the “secularization thesis”
strands.focus: Social criticism and clerical doubt read as stages of secularization from the 1880s, with the 1920s as an era of drift. “Secularization thesis” is the critics’ name (Laverdure’s review of Christie and Gauvreau); Marshall defended the concept against Gauvreau in 1993–94 as a long-term, incremental process.
strands.works: Cook (1985); Marshall, Secularizing the Faith (1992); Marshall, “Canadian Historians, Secularization and the Problem of the Nineteenth Century” (1993–94)

strands.title: Revisionists: churches at their height before 1940
strands.focus: The evangelical creed accommodated modern thought, and the Protestant churches were at their greatest cultural influence before 1940; secularization belongs after the Second World War. Marshall (1993–94) names Gauvreau and Van Die as critics of the thesis.
strands.works: Van Die (1989); Gauvreau, The Evangelical Century (1991); Christie and Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996)

strands.title: Lived religion: congregation, gender, leisure, irreligion
strands.focus: From clergy and doctrine to lay practice: Protestant culture, Methodism as a national church, class and gender in church and leisure, irreligion in settler British Columbia, and political versus social secularization.
strands.works: Westfall (1989); Semple (1996); Marks (1996, 2017); Christie, ed. (2001); Christie and Gauvreau (2010); Van Die (2014)

strands.title: Catholicism, Rome and ethnicity
strands.focus: Syntheses of Quebec Catholicism, Rome and Canadian affairs, Irish Catholic Toronto and the Church's management of rites.
strands.works: Hamelin and Gagnon (1984); Perin (1990); McGowan (1999); Ferretti (1999); Hubert (2000)

strands.title: Comparisons: British secularization and moral reform
strands.focus: Brown's 1960s rupture is the international reference for the revisionist chronology; Valverde's moral reform is the regulatory neighbour of the social gospel.

extension_coverage.note: Uptake is declining (answer to Q16). The share of the 1,303 strict History PhDs (2009–26) citing two or more of the listed works fell from 7.8% (2009–14) to 4.4% (2020–26); on the cross-group measure in answers/data-answers.json the 2020–26 share is 0.69 of the 2009–14 share (0.67 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), below the median of 0.73 for all groups, while median bibliography length grew (233.5 to 252 entries). Allen’s Social Passion fell from 1.5% to 0.5% of PhDs. Post-2000 works are selected milestones, not a reviewed field.

relation_to_periods: Main-period entry (period_2) whose debate runs into period_3; the Catholic Action strand moved to quebec_historiography (2026-10-12).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Religious thought as Canadian intellectual history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Gauvreau's Evangelical Century treats the evangelical creed as "the intellectual expression" of Protestant culture and was presented as transforming how Canadian intellectual history is read; Marshall's summary calls secularization "a key development in Canadian religious and intellectual history". Comparison: much of the field is social rather than intellectual history.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Social-history methods turn the field toward lay practice
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Marks studies church and leisure participation by class and gender in three Ontario towns; Christie and Gauvreau subtitle their 2010 synthesis "A Social History of Religion in Canada". Neither names the new social history as a source; the contribution is of method and subject, not an influence claim.

Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. PhD context: 25 of 42 PhDs citing The Regenerators also cite Valverde (lift 7.2). Comparison only; target is proposed.
proposed_relationships.coordination: Duplicates mreg_rel_04 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform comparison) in the moral_regulation draft. Keep one edge and merge the evidence notes.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Catholic Action revisionism reinterprets the Quiet Revolution
proposed_relationships.map_label: Catholic origins of the Quiet Revolution
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Gauvreau's review: Quebec religious history had repeated "the conventional ideology of the Quiet Revolution" until Catholic Action studies shifted attention to laypeople; Baum sets out the social-democratic (Meunier and Warren) and family-and-gender (Gauvreau) versions. PhD context: 16 of the 47 PhDs citing Gauvreau (2005) and 14 of 22 citing Bienvenue are at francophone universities. Target is proposed.
proposed_relationships.coordination: Kept after the Catholic Action strand moved to quebec_historiography (answer to Q12): the contribution now runs from Gauvreau’s home field to the strand quebec_historiography/catholic_action_origins. The quebec_historiography draft keeps its broad comparison qcreq_rel_06; the atlas allows the two to coexist (cf. edge_041/edge_369).

proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Hébert: monographs on pre-1960 youth movements (including Bienvenue and Gauvreau) sought to refute the idea that before '68 there was no salvation. Baum: Gauvreau carries Catholic Action's values into 1960s marriage and the refusal of Humanae vitae (1968). Shared works inflate the PhD overlap between the two drafts (lift 4.2), so it is not cited as evidence. Target is proposed.

Marks's chapters on church ladies, freethinkers and working-class women in the Salvation Army; Gauvreau on Catholic Action, the family and women's desire (per Baum); Households of Faith on separate spheres, masculinity, fatherhood and personalist feminism. Comparison only; target is proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Religion as a vehicle of the liberal order
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Christie: work on the Protestant churches and New Liberalism means no one "can ignore religion as a powerful vehicle in the creation of the liberal order"; the Catholic church also articulated liberal values. She offers this as an extension that also criticizes McKay's neglect of religion. Van Die's political versus social secularization is set within the "liberal state"; Christie's Households of Faith (2001) opens with "the Rise of Liberal Society" and closes on "Canada’s Liberal Tradition", before McKay's framework was debated. Target is proposed.

open_questions: Should the Catholic Action and Quiet Revolution strand live here, in Quebec historiography, or in Canada's 1960s? The draft keeps the works here and links them to both by contribution.
Are Cook and Marshall well described as the "secularization thesis"? The label comes from Laverdure's 1998 review; Marshall's 1993 historiographical essay (unverified) would give his own account.
Allen's The Social Passion is cited by only 16 PhDs (2009–26) and is falling; is it still the right founding milestone, or should the label start with Cook (1985)?
Should Irish Catholic and ethnic religious history (Clarke, McGowan, Perin) move to immigration and ethnicity?
Engagement falls from 7.8% (2009–14) to 4.4% (2020–26) of PhDs citing two or more of the listed works; should the field be described as declining in the extension coverage note?

Gauvreau stays here as primary.
